LONDON, Nov 6 : Uncertainty over the growth outlook and expectations that inflation will remain elevated next year are weighing on global markets, even as hopes of a de-escalation in the Iran war have eased oil prices. Government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year, confidence in the AI boom is faltering and European economic data has softened. The combination is fuelling concern that inflation could stay high even as growth slows, although the Democratic victory in US midterm elections has raised hopes for an eventual end to the Iran war. OIL STILL HIGH

Oil has fallen almost 20 per cent this week to below $100 a barrel. But analysts warn that any resolution to the Iran war remains uncertain, leaving scope for prices to rise again. Oil is still up almost 60 per cent this year, while natural gas remains nearly three times its level at the start of 2026. That backdrop is keeping near-term inflation expectations elevated and reinforcing concerns that price pressures could persist as growth slows, forcing central banks to raise interest rates further. The University of Michigan's measure of one-year US inflation expectations edged up to 4.7 per cent in October from 4.6 per cent in September and 3.4 per cent in February. Market measures of long-term inflation expectations remain above 2 per cent in the euro zone and the US, and above 3 per cent in Britain. Higher energy costs add to inflation while also weighing on growth by increasing transport, manufacturing and household expenses. AllianceBernstein chief investment strategist Inigo Fraser Jenkins said the geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions driving inflationary pressures would persist beyond the US midterms. "Today it's oil, but next time it could be cobalt, lithium or something else, and we need to get used to that," he said. "It will manifest itself in the form of higher inflation and greater volatility." FOOD PRICES BITE Food prices, driven higher by extreme weather, shipping disruptions and elevated energy costs, remain a key inflation concern. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization's Food Price Index is at its highest level in nearly four years. Costs could rise further, with major consumer goods and food companies warning of price increases to offset higher expenses, while Britain's leading retail trade body has flagged similar concerns. Food inflation can also fuel broader economic pressures, said Hank Calenti, global markets strategist at SMBC. "Food inflation makes people start to think that 'there's really inflation here and it's going to stay high and I need to get a better job or my employer needs to pay me more'," he said. "So, those second-round effects come in." TIGHTER FINANCING CONDITIONS Analysts say tighter financial conditions are another reason for caution on the growth outlook. US government borrowing costs surged 85 basis points in the third quarter, while those in France and Italy jumped more than 100 bps. Although yields have eased since then, they remain sharply higher this year. Demand for safe-haven German bonds should help contain borrowing costs across the euro zone. But a widening spread between French and German debt could tighten financing conditions without any change in European Central Bank policy. ECB estimates circulated before last Thursday's policy meeting showed the latest rise in bond yields would reduce economic growth by a cumulative 100 bps in 2027-28 compared with September projections. TECH PAIN WILL BE FELT Another sign of tighter financial conditions has been a selloff in risk assets, particularly AI-related stocks. Major stock indexes remain close to record highs, but investors are increasingly questioning the strength of the AI boom and watching the decline in technology shares closely. More than $2 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq 100's market value last month alone. Further declines could erode household wealth, raise corporate funding costs and curb investors' appetite for risk, potentially weighing on future investment. "Financial conditions tightened last week as credit spreads widened, and equity prices fell. But Fed (US Federal Reserve) officials may not yet be ready to conclude they are sufficiently restrictive," Citi said in a note. DATA PICTURE SOFTENS Economic growth in the euro zone slowed sharply in October as demand came close to stalling, while rising costs squeezed businesses and confidence fell to its lowest level in five months, data showed on Wednesday. Citi's European economic surprise index, which measures whether data beat or missed expectations, is also pointing lower. US growth remains resilient, supported in part by heavy investment in AI infrastructure. RJ Gallo, chief investment officer for global fixed income at Federated Hermes, cautioned against overusing the term stagflation, which describes a combination of high inflation, weak growth and elevated unemployment. He noted that the US economy continues to grow at a solid pace and that unemployment, at 4.2 per cent, remains low by historical standards, adding that "inflation continues to be the Fed's primary concern".

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Japanese investors bought foreign long-term bonds for the first time in seven weeks in the week ended October 31, opting for safety amid a selloff in technology stocks and after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady. These investors shrugged off earlier concerns about rising energy costs and government debt as the AI trade slipped over disappointing earnings from some top companies. Traders were watching for signs that enough money was returning home to move Japan's domestic and foreign markets. Japanese investors bought a net 1.31 trillion yen ($8.31 billion) of foreign long-term bonds after withdrawing a combined 3.51 trillion yen over a six-week selling streak, data from Japan's Ministry of Finance showed. They, however, sold a net 209.3 billion yen of foreign short-term bills.

COLOMBO, Nov 6 : Sri Lanka will use next week's budget to convince investors its economic recovery can outlast a four-year International Monetary Fund bailout that is nearing an end, while trying to revive growth and cushion households from surging energy prices. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, who also holds the finance portfolio, will present the budget for 2027 on November 12, laying the groundwork for the island nation's return to bond markets after exiting a $2.9 billion IMF programme in March. His challenge will be to shift the economy from crisis-era stabilisation towards stronger investment and growth without undermining the fiscal discipline that helped pull the country back from its worst economic crisis in decades. Sri Lanka's turnaround since 2022 has been stark.

It went from running out of foreign exchange, struggling to import fuel, food and medicines and defaulting on its foreign debt to rebuilding reserves and recording sustained economic growth. The economic collapse also triggered mass street protests that forced then-President Gotabaya Rajapaksa to flee the country and resign after demonstrators stormed his official residence, bringing an abrupt end to a presidency dominated by his powerful family. The economy has now expanded for 12 consecutive quarters, while gross official reserves reached $6.9 billion by the end of October. "No country has ever done enough," said Evan Papageorgiou, the IMF's mission chief for Sri Lanka, in an interview. "So let's put it like this - Sri Lanka has done quite a lot, but more needs to be done so that this transformation can go from stabilization to prosperity." "We think the central test is whether the budget safeguards fiscal and debt sustainability while still creating space for the development priorities we'll be discussing." Sri Lanka approaches the budget unveiling with stronger public finances after recording a primary surplus of 5.4 per cent of gross domestic product in 2025. The government's fiscal strategy targets a 2.6 per cent surplus in 2027 and seeks to narrow the overall deficit to 4.5 per cent of GDP. The government is targeting revenue and grants of 15.5 per cent of GDP, including tax revenue of 14.2 per cent, while keeping public investment above 4 per cent of GDP. But Dissanayake is also under pressure to protect households from inflation after the US-Israeli war on Iran pushed up energy costs. Inflation in Colombo, the capital, accelerated to 8.3 per cent in October. The government has already rolled out fuel and electricity subsidies, cash assistance to low-income households and support for farmers and fishermen. POST-IMF PRESSURES Despite the rebound, the World Bank says the recovery remains "incomplete and uneven." It expects growth of 4.4 per cent this year and 4.2 per cent in 2027, while the poverty level, estimated at 16.9 per cent in 2025, remains above pre-crisis levels. "There's a need to really begin to shift towards a different type of growth model," said Jakob Engel, a senior country economist at the World Bank, calling for a move from public investment and debt-driven growth towards private-sector investment, exports and productivity. The budget is also a condition for completing the seventh review of the IMF programme, which would unlock about $345 million and take total disbursements to around $2.7 billion. Investor confidence has improved, with Fitch Ratings upgrading Sri Lanka to B-minus from CCC-plus in September, citing stronger fiscal and external balances, reforms and rebuilding reserves. But it warned debt and debt-service burdens remained high. Sri Lanka, which last issued international bonds in 2019, could still face steep borrowing costs. Economist and former central bank Deputy Governor W.A. Wijewardena estimated borrowing costs could reach 11 per cent to 12 per cent. "This is not an affordable interest rate for a country like Sri Lanka," he said. "If we have to borrow at these rates, we will be driven back into the old debt trap."

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Nov 6 : Japan's economy is expected to have expanded only marginally between July-September, as recoveries in capital spending were largely offset by slowdowns in private consumption and external demand, a Reuters poll showed on Friday. • Real gross domestic product (GDP) likely grew an annualised 0.3 per cent in the third quarter, according to the median forecast of 16 economists, slowing from a 1.4 per cent expansion in April-June but remaining on track for a fourth straight quarterly increase. • Without annualisation, the July-September growth rate was estimated at 0.1 per cent. • Economic growth will be among factors considered by the Bank of Japan in deciding whether to raise interest rates further. BEIJING/PERTH Nov 6 : Oil prices are set for a sharp weekly drop on expectations of a de-escalation of the Iran war after US President Donald Trump's party suffered election losses, but Middle East supply concerns from the conflict continue to provide a floor for the market. Brent crude futures for January rose on Friday by $1.29, or 1.31 per cent, to $99.58 a barrel as of 0504 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures climbed 86 cents, or 0.95 per cent, to $91.38 a barrel. Brent briefly breached the $100-a-barrel mark in morning trade. Both contracts gained for a second day. Still, the Brent contract is on track to drop by 12 per cent this week after the December contract expired on October 30, while WTI is set to drop 12.1 per cent.

The contracts plunged earlier this week on expectations that US midterm elections on Tuesday, which swung the Senate and House of Representatives to the Democratic Party from Trump's Republicans, could lead to a de-escalation of the US-Israeli war against Iran, now in its ninth month. Oil prices fell 8 per cent on Wednesday alone after the Democrats swept the elections, settling at two-month lows. However, prices rebounded on a surge in tanker attacks on Wednesday and Thursday in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz — the crucial sea outlet for a majority of Middle Eastern oil shipments — that renewed the concerns about supply flows from the region. KCM chief analyst Tim Waterer described Friday's rise as a "technical recovery" from the steep selloff after the US elections, but said the underlying driver was a realisation that the problem had not disappeared and attacks in the Strait of Hormuz were unaffected by a Democratic win. "Until there is a credible path to safer, cheaper transit through the Gulf, oil is likely to remain supported on dips and prone to sharp moves on any escalation headlines," he said. Nov 5 : Trump-backed cryptocurrency venture World Liberty Financial said on Thursday it was launching a buyback programme for its WLFI governance token, funded by an initial allocation that could include revenue generated from reserves backing its USD1 stablecoin and other sources. The announcement comes after the WLFI token came under pressure following the Republican Party's weaker-than-expected performance in this week's US midterm elections. The token has fallen about 10 per cent since the vote and is down more than 60 per cent so far this year, according to CoinMarketCap.com. The company said the program is intended to encourage participation in WLFI governance and increase voting power among long-term token holders. It added that token buybacks are intended to become an ongoing part of its strategy. World Liberty was co-founded in 2024 by President Donald Trump, his three sons and a group of partners. The Trump family owns 38 per cent of World Liberty and makes money through the sale or use of its crypto tokens, the $WLFI governance token and USD1 stablecoin.

While the historic "blue wave" in Tuesday's vote had been initially welcomed on hopes it could put pressure on President Donald Trump to wind down his war against Iran, fears about the impact on the AI buildout soon came to the fore. Seoul dived 8.5 per cent at one point, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes, with chip giant SK hynix off 10 per cent while rival Samsung was 8 per cent down. The administration is also looking for non-tax revenue as it seeks to bankroll an ambitious spending push. Takaichi said the government, for one, will use proceeds from the BOJ's increased sales of its ETF holdings to fund spending on areas critical to the country's economic security. "Additional proceeds from the (ETF) sales are fruits of Japan's economic growth, so it's appropriate to reinvest them for spending on crisis management and growth areas," she said. The BOJ kept interest rates steady last month but stressed its resolve to focus on inflation risks, reinforcing market bets on a rate hike as soon as December. It has also described financial conditions as loose due in part to a weak yen and rising stock prices, which lift manufacturers' profits and incentivise them to boost investment. "Unless the yen spikes in a way that eases inflationary pressure, the BOJ will probably stay its course and keep raising rates," said Naomi Muguruma, chief bond strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities. "But the market rout may give the BOJ an excuse to take a wait-and-see stance for longer than expected. It will certainly make its communication leading up to December difficult." The roadshow was initially expected to kick off the week of November 9, Reuters previously reported, with pricing expected the following week. Investors are also eagerly awaiting Anthropic's October revenue figure, which the company left blank in its updated S-1 filing, to assess whether the AI lab has managed to boost growth after a slowdown in recent months, two of the people said.  Wall Street and Silicon Valley were abuzz on Thursday with questions about whether the company would move forward, in the wake of the two-day AI market selloff following Tuesday’s US midterm elections. A decision to delay the offering would likely fuel further concern over the health of the AI ecosystem at a time when the success of ballot efforts in many states limiting data center development has crystallized political opposition to data centers and other aspects of AI. An Anthropic delay could also pose a threat to the broader stock market, which is heavily weighted toward large technology firms whose valuations would likely be squeezed by any sense that Anthropic, one of the highest-profile AI firms, is finding it difficult to raise funds. At one point this year its IPO was expected by investors to take place in October and to seek a valuation as high as $2 trillion. Some analysts say that Anthropic, like SpaceX before it, is likely to benefit from strong retail investor demand. "It's not like these companies are not going to be a part of the future," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey. "They're going to become public. Investors are still going to have a lot of interest in them. Valuations have risen for a long time in the private market, and we'll probably see some pullback." Even if Anthropic and its investors get together on a valuation, as Wall Street currently expects, other factors could determine whether the company chooses to move forward with the IPO by year-end. If the market for AI-related assets remains under pressure, the company could decide to delay the offering until the market looks more resilient and likely to smoothly digest an offering that is expected by some to reach $100 billion, the people familiar with investor discussions said. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday evening that IPO investors are skeptical Anthropic can achieve $1.5 trillion in valuation in a public listing. MARKET ROUT TESTS AI CONFIDENCE Trading was anything but smooth on Thursday, fueled by the outcome this week at the polls but also by corporate developments and increasing market anxiety. Microsoft tightened oversight of some data center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Nebius, Iren and CoreWeave were among the biggest decliners on Thursday and each has lost half their market value over the past month. Meanwhile investors fled from all AI-related assets, with the credit default swaps covering CoreWeave and SpaceX alike hitting records that imply an increasing expectation that they could default on their obligations in coming years. More than 50 S&P 1500 technology stocks dropped by 10 per cent or more, and Vanda Research said retail selling was the strongest it has been since the COVID-19 pandemic. "We are now seeing something of a buyers' strike in tech," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta. Tech has underperformed the S&P 500 by 10.7 per cent over the past month, the most extreme one-month underperformance since May 2002, Lerner said. He described the selling so far as uncomfortable but not abnormal, while adding, "the rubber band is getting stretched."

TOKYO, Nov 6 : For years, Japanese savers left their cash in bank accounts that paid next to nothing because few things paid much more. With government bonds now yielding four times as much as deposits, that no longer holds and banks are starting to worry. When the Bank of Japan last week declared victory in its near 14-year battle to lift inflation to its 2 per cent target, it closed a long chapter of near-zero interest rates. Now, rising bond yields are making households more sensitive to returns on their money, fuelling a boom in government bond purchases and prompting some to shift a portion of the $7 trillion they hold out of bank deposits. Takashi Kamachi, a 46-year-old self-employed businessman in Osaka, recently moved 600,000 yen ($3,785.01) of his teenage son's gift money, held for years in a Japan Post Bank account, into retail government bonds (JGBs).

"Banks are promoting time deposits again, but I thought government bonds looked far more attractive, perhaps four or five times better in terms of returns," he said. To be sure, the shift is still modest. However, policymakers hope households will eventually play a bigger role in funding Japan's massive budget as stable holders of government debt, and help fill a hole left by the BOJ's diminishing JGB purchases. "Foreign investors can help fill the gap, but what Japan really needs is a stable buyer base, and that means households," said Kenji Nakanishi, a senior ruling party lawmaker and key advocate of expanding retail ownership of government bonds. 'INTEREST RATES EXIST' Retail Japanese government bond sales in the April-October period have nearly doubled from a year earlier to 6 trillion yen. Over last three consecutive months, monthly sales have exceeded 1 trillion yen, as yields on popular retail bonds climbed above 2 per cent, far outstripping bank deposit rates that mostly remain below 1 per cent. "People are starting to realise that interest rates exist," said Takayuki Nakagawa, general manager of retail marketing at SBI Securities, Japan's largest seller of retail government bonds. Many buyers are first-time investors seeking a safe alternative to bank deposits, according to Nakagawa. Drawn by a government guarantee of principal, they represent the same conservative savers banks have traditionally relied on for funding, he said. Despite the BOJ lifting its policy rates, commercial banks have kept deposit rates low to minimise funding costs, offering around 0.5 per cent on one-year deposits, not enough to beat inflation. In contrast, 3- and 5-year retail notes and 10-year floaters all offer coupons above 2 per cent. Japanese households hold roughly 2.50 quadrillion yen in financial assets, according to BOJ data, with cash and deposits accounting for about 1.13 quadrillion yen. Even with that demand, household holdings of government bonds account for less than 1 per cent of their financial assets, compared with roughly 2 per cent for US households' holdings of Treasury securities. JGBs must also compete with global and domestic equities, which have already attracted a steady stream of funds from younger investors seeking higher returns. Eager to find sources of revenue to fund their spending, some lawmakers want to make JGBs more attractive, such as through longer-duration products and incentives such as inheritance-tax benefits. "Now that momentum is finally building, this is exactly the time to give it an extra push," Nakanishi said. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama wants to improve the appeal of retail government bonds. Her ministry, for one, is studying the launch of additional retail bond products, it said on Thursday, while also calling for discussions on preferential tax treatment for buyers. PUSHBACK The idea, however, faces pushback from some lawmakers who fret it would widen income disparity by benefiting already wealthy households. Meanwhile, commercial banks fear a shift into bonds could drain deposits, leaving less ammunition to profit from increasing borrowing demand. Some bank officials say they are already seeing once loyal customers shift money into JGBs. "Preferential treatment for retail government bonds would be a problem," said a senior regional bank official, who requested anonymity. Bank lending has consistently outpaced deposit growth this year, with loans rising 5-6 per cent from a year earlier while deposits grew only around 2 per cent, according to BOJ data, forcing lenders to compete more aggressively for household savings. "A rapid and excessive shift of funds from bank deposits into retail government bonds could weaken the credit-creation function banks are responsible for and affect their ability to supply growth capital to the economy," Mizuho Bank head Masahiko Kato, who is also chair of a banking lobby, said in September. There are also questions about financing Japan's huge debt with household savings. Foreign investors have increased their presence in the JGB market, raising concerns that yields could become more vulnerable to sharp swings in global sentiment. The BOJ's share of the JGB and T-bill market has fallen to 41.2 per cent in June 2026 from a peak of 47.9 per cent in December 2023, as it tapered bond purchases to unwind monetary stimulus. Banks' share has more than halved to 17.8 per cent since 2013, when the BOJ deployed a huge asset-buying scheme. Takero Doi, a professor at Keio University, said instead of boosting retail bond demand, policymakers should focus on reducing government debt. "You could simply end up seeing households replacing banks as buyers of retail government bonds," he said. "That won't solve the underlying problem." ($1 = 158.5200 yen)

HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue.  Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance – informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell. In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48 per cent. THE BLAME GAME So who’s been selling? The blame game has already begun.

Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge funds, has pointed the finger at insurers. In a recent letter to clients, founder Hong Liang accused the insurance firms of piling into technology stocks near their July peak, only to slash positions in late September. The behaviour was “truly baffling”, lamented the prominent investor, who has a large following on the mainland. Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time. China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the United States, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound.  NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness.  That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

Related:

Commentary: Beijing cracks down on cross-border investment but it is up to something grander

Commentary: What China’s underperforming tech stocks say about its real economy

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance, for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2 per cent of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9 per cent in 2025.  Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market – a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.  In recent days, authorities have issued window guidance to several major insurers, requiring them to report their equity holdings, refrain from cutting their losses, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals. WHO WILL BE LEFT TO BLAME? The government now appears to be grappling with an unintended consequence of its own policy.  Insurers may be more patient investors than hedge funds, but they still have to manage risk and meet claims and other liabilities. That limits their ability to sit indefinitely on mounting losses – and can force them to cut exposure during severe market downturns.  Insurers, in other words, cannot be as reliably countercyclical as the “national team”, whose primary purpose is market stabilisation.

Related:

Commentary: China is betting on spreading AI faster than the US can contain it

Commentary: This bad movie is a good guide to China’s stock market

On its latest earnings call, executives at China Pacific Insurance Group acknowledged that equity investing had become “complicated” and that portfolios needed to be managed so market volatility didn’t damage short-term returns. In the third quarter, profits at China’s five major listed insurers plunged, largely because of the decline in domestic stocks. The experience points to an uncomfortable reality: For insurers, reliable dividend payers such as Bank of Jiangsu may ultimately be better suited to their liabilities than capital-intensive chipmakers. Few in China – including Shiva’s Liang – are willing to say publicly that policy missteps themselves may be contributing to poor stock market performance. Instead, blame has fallen on everything from thin liquidity to indiscriminate selling. But that raises a bigger question: Why does China keep suffering stock market routs? Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts – in 2018, 2024 and now. The next time the PBOC has to put out a fire, who will be left to blame? Foreigners, hedge funds and now even state-owned insurers have all had their turn.

Nov 5 : AI data center firm IREN on Thursday delayed some infrastructure deliveries for Microsoft and laid out another $15 billion in spending, even as a rout in AI stocks puts the sector's massive buildout under pressure. Australia-based IREN also beat quarterly revenue estimates on strong growth in its AI cloud business, lifting its shares 4 per cent in extended trading. The stock closed down about 17 per cent during a broader selloff that hit chipmakers and so-called neocloud companies, including IREN rival CoreWeave, particularly hard as Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterms fanned fears of tougher regulation of the technology. IREN said the delay to infrastructure being built for Microsoft would not result in financial penalties as it stemmed from the software giant requesting network-design changes. However, the company pushed the timeline for making operational its more than $4 billion annualized run-rate revenue target to January from year-end, and said the timing could extend to the end of February. The company said the shift followed a customer-requested design change and supplier timing.

The Windows maker is tightening oversight of some data center projects run by neocloud providers including IREN, Nebius and Nscale amid delays and rising costs, Bloomberg News reported earlier on Thursday. Microsoft is stepping away from projects it considers risky and weighing whether to sign new deals with such providers as it focuses more heavily on expanding its own data centers, according to the report. IREN, valued at some $7 billion, is building 200 megawatts of data-center capacity for Microsoft in Texas. The company said it would keep investing significantly in computing equipment and infrastructure as it expands its AI cloud business, estimating about $15 billion in capital expenditure over the rest of its fiscal year. Its quarterly filing showed capital commitments of $18.95 billion at the end of September, up from $13.81 billion three months earlier, while GPU hardware on its balance sheet nearly tripled to $5.82 billion from $2.04 billion. Construction in progress stood at about $4.61 billion. IREN's AI cloud revenue in the first quarter rose to $200 million from $71 million in the prior three months. Total revenue rose to $228 million in the quarter ended September 30, compared with analysts' average estimate of $221.28 million, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company said its assets and revenue were supported by contracts with Nvidia, Microsoft and 13 others, with roughly two-thirds of its revenue backlog tied to investment-grade counterparties. IREN executives said on a post-earnings call that the company exited September with $1 billion in annualized run-rate revenue and expects roughly one-quarter of that amount to be recognized in the December quarter.
